book.title: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
book.author: Ramit Sethi

confidence_note: Mechanics (accounts, 5th/7th schedule, 5-10 percent savings, about 10 percent Roth IRA, $500 buffer, opt-out study) come from Sethi's own website page on automation and summaries; not checked against the 2009 text, and the study figures are his citation of a 401(k) result. The old text's interviews of hundreds of people and its 'even the least disciplined get rich' promise were dropped. The 4-bucket list and percentage ranges are from reviews.
facts: Sethi: 'It's not about willpower'; automation reduces the daily decisions that lead people to do nothing.
He cites a 401(k) study: making enrollment opt-out instead of opt-in raised contribution rates from under 40 percent to nearly 100 percent (a retirement-enrollment result).
Step 1: link accounts (401(k) to checking via direct deposit; checking to Roth IRA, savings, credit card). Step 2: ask companies to move bill dates to payday.

Example with payday on the 1st: 401(k) portion withheld, take-home to checking with a $500 buffer at first; on the 5th transfers to savings (typically 5-10 percent of income per his plan) and Roth IRA (roughly 10 percent of take-home); on the 7th autopay for recurring bills.
He prefers paying bills by credit card, then paying the card in full from checking, with an email notification to review the statement first; if you cannot afford the savings figure, start with $5.
Conscious spending plan buckets: fixed costs, savings, investments, guilt-free spending; what remains is yours to spend.
scene_details: email notice before the card statement is paid
tension: People who mean to save still do nothing; he removes the monthly decision instead of asking for discipline.
opening_idea: Open on the paycheck arriving on the 1st and everything settled by the 7th with no decision made.

lessons.idea: Put a recurring decision into a one-time setup.
lessons.example: A shop owner sets supplier payment on a fixed date instead of paying by hand.

reflect_final: Which recurring decision in your week or month do you keep remaking by hand, and what would one single setup that runs without you look like?

use_cases.situation: A month ended with nothing set aside.
use_cases.move: Set one transfer for the day after payday, as in Sethi's 5th-of-the-month transfer, and see what's left.

use_cases.situation: A couple argues about saving every month.
use_cases.move: Agree on the amount once and let the transfer run.

use_cases.situation: A friend says they will start saving next month.
use_cases.move: Mention the opt-out study and propose a $5 transfer now.

pocket_idea: Set the transfer for the day after payday; decide once and the month stops asking.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Money moved by the 7th with no decision made.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Not willpower; paycheck on the 1st, automatic transfers on the 5th, autopay on the 7th; opt-out study.
